source: Zhu et al. (2024) Conformity in Large Language Models
finding: The authors rebuilt Asch's design as multiple-choice dialogue. Confederates unanimously give a wrong answer before the model answers. All four tested open models conformed to some degree, on objective and subjective tasks.
numbers: Models: Gemma2-9B, Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Qwen2-7B, base and instruct. Datasets: CommonsenseQA, MMLU, PopQA, BBH Object Counting (objective); Politiscale, OpinionsQA (subjective). 2 to 10 confederates. Greedy decoding.
limits: Small open models only (7-9B). Multiple-choice, text-only. Numeric rates are in figures, not text.
agent_relevance: G5 is real for small models: a stated unanimous wrong answer pulls the answer. Do not show the model prior answers of others before it decides.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Conformity in Large Language Models
finding: Conformity comes from unanimity, not from the dialogue format. A diverse wrong crowd (confederates split across wrong answers) gives much less conformity than a unanimous one.
numbers: Figure 3: Unanimous vs Diverse incorrect answers, MMLU, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, 2 to 10 participants.
limits: Same small-model limits.
agent_relevance: Agreement among copies is the dangerous case. Unanimous voters from one model carry no extra evidence (supports G4).

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Conformity in Large Language Models
finding: Tone matters. A conversational (Neutral) wording raises conformity versus a Plain list of answers. A Confident tone raises it further. An Uncertain tone has a weaker effect.
numbers: Figure 4: Plain vs Neutral vs Uncertain vs Confident, unanimous setting, MMLU, four models.
limits: Direction reported in text; effect sizes in figure only.
agent_relevance: Strip tone from any peer or earlier-attempt text before the model sees it. Pass bare answers, not confident prose.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Conformity in Large Language Models
finding: Instruction tuning reduces conformity. Gemma2 and Llama-3 fall significantly. Mistral and Qwen2 change little because they already conformed little.
numbers: Figure 5: base vs instruct, Unanimous-Plain, MMLU.
limits: Only 4 families. Other studies (Sharma) show RLHF can also raise sycophancy.
agent_relevance: Stronger post-training helps but does not remove the effect; keep the scaffold-level guard.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Conformity in Large Language Models
finding: Harder tasks produce more conformity. Conformity level correlates strongly and negatively with the model's own accuracy per subject.
numbers: Pearson r = -0.777 across 57 MMLU subjects, Llama-3-8B-Instruct. BBH Object Counting (hard) showed more conformity than easier tasks.
limits: Correlation over subjects, one model.
agent_relevance: Expect the guard to matter most exactly where the model is weakest (hard items).

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Conformity in Large Language Models
finding: Initial confidence predicts resistance. Questions never conformed to had higher pre-pressure confidence (option log probability on MMLU; EigV consistency on PopQA). Low initial confidence leads to following the majority.
numbers: MMLU and PopQA, p < 0.001 for the difference in confidence distributions.
limits: Needs logprobs or sampled consistency.
agent_relevance: A cheap signal: low self-consistency before seeing others means the answer is likely to be overwritten by social input.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Conformity in Large Language Models
finding: Devil's Advocate: adding one extra dissenting confederate cuts conformity, even when the dissenter is also wrong. Question Distillation: replacing the list of repeated answers with one summary line also cuts it. Attention maps show less attention on the majority answer.
numbers: Figure 8 (MMLU, 2-10 participants): DA and QD both lower conformity versus original, mostly for Gemma2 and Llama-3. DA also worked on subjective OpinionsQA.
limits: Prompt-level patches, tested on 7-9B models only. Gains are larger for the more susceptible models.
agent_relevance: Cheap prompt-side fixes: never repeat the majority claim; summarise it once. A dissenting voice need not be correct to break unanimity.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Conformity in Large Language Models
finding: Same devil's-advocate trick lowers sycophancy on TriviaQA with a user-suggested wrong answer.
numbers: Table 3, Llama-3-8B base: sycophantic 63.20% to 41.37%, correct 36.80% to 57.82%. Instruct: sycophantic 25.18% to 12.37%, correct 74.82% to 87.62%.
limits: One dataset, one model family.
agent_relevance: Links conformity and sycophancy as one mechanism, so one guard can cover both.

source: Choi et al. (2025) An Empirical Study of Group Conformity in Multi-Agent Systems
finding: Neutral-disposition agents in debates drift toward the numerically larger group and toward the more capable group.
numbers: Over 2,500 debate simulations on 5 contentious topics. Chi-square: majority effect chi2 = 164.839 (df 1, p < 0.001); intelligence effect chi2 = 142.285 (df 1, p < 0.001). Welch ANOVA: majority eta2p about 0.068 (moderate), intelligence eta2p about 0.1665 (large).
limits: Opinion topics, not factual tasks. Judge role is GPT-4o. Model 'intelligence' is a proxy via model family/size.
agent_relevance: Capability of the voice matters more than headcount. A fluent strong source overrides the agent; a weak agent should not trust a stronger one blindly without a check.

source: Choi et al. (2025) An Empirical Study of Group Conformity in Multi-Agent Systems
finding: One high-capability agent moves the neutral agent more than a larger low-capability group. Full conformity (adopting the stance completely) also occurs. Weaker models' conformity scales with majority size; GPT-4o-mini shows a weaker size relation.
numbers: Figure 2 bubble plots: smaller-but-smarter group beats larger-but-weaker group. Models: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3-Sonnet, Claude-3-Haiku, Qwen.
quote: Authors link results to Asch 1955 for full conformity.
limits: Trends consistent across all five topics.
agent_relevance: Headcount is a poor evidence signal in both humans and LLMs; the scaffold should weigh checked evidence, not votes.

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Debate often lowers group accuracy over rounds, even when stronger models outnumber weaker ones. Agents flip from correct to incorrect more often than the reverse.
numbers: Tasks: MMLU, CommonsenseQA, GSM8K. Mixes of GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B. 100 random samples, 5 seeds, mean and s.e. Correct-to-incorrect transitions exceed incorrect-to-correct in later rounds.
limits: Small samples (100 per cell). Exact per-cell numbers in figures/tables.
agent_relevance: Exchanging reasons between copies can overwrite right answers. Supports G4 and G5.

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Social pressure dose-response: an agent's chance of flipping from correct to wrong is highest when no peer agrees with it and falls as more peers agree. Resistance to flipping also drops from round 1 to round 2.
numbers: Figure 4: flip likelihood versus number of agreeing peers, averaged over rounds; large variance by dataset and model (on GSM8K, GPT and Mistral flip far less than LLaMA).
limits: Observational; not a controlled Asch design.
agent_relevance: Isolation is the risk state. A lone correct answer facing a disagreeing pool is the worst case for the agent.

source: Yao et al. (2025) Peacemaker or Troublemaker: How Sycophancy Shapes Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Inter-agent sycophancy collapses disagreement before a correct answer is reached, and debate then scores below single-agent baselines. A disagreement collapse rate (DCR) metric is introduced.
numbers: Decentralized Llama3.3-70B homogeneous DCR up to 86.36% (2-agent CommonsenseQA). Centralized judge: Qwen-Qwen and Qwen-Llama accuracy 83.62% and 81.00% to 86.65% and 86.49%; DCR 81.71% and 80.41% to 41.27% and 35.51%.
limits: Two datasets; judge-driven failures also exist; 3-agent centralized gains are smaller.
agent_relevance: Add a code-counted disagreement-collapse check; a neutral judge reduces collapse.

source: Yao et al. (2025) Peacemaker or Troublemaker: How Sycophancy Shapes Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Prompting agents toward 'peacemaker' (high sycophancy) or 'troublemaker' (low) personas changes accuracy. More sycophancy generally hurts; low-sycophancy pairs in a cross-model debate did best.
numbers: Homogeneous Qwen-Qwen: 81.98% to 83.87% over 45 persona configs, worst at both peacemaker. Heterogeneous Qwen3-32B/Llama3-70B: 78.95% to 82.06% over 81 configs, best at both troublemaker.
limits: Small spreads (a few points). Personas conflict with our G4 (no persona voters) but are used here as a manipulation, not as voters.
agent_relevance: Anti-sycophancy instructions give a few points at most; structure (judge, heterogeneity) matters more.

source: Laban et al. (2023) Are You Sure? Challenging LLMs Leads to Performance Drops in the FlipFlop Experiment
finding: A bare challenge ('Are you sure?') makes models abandon answers. Models flip on average 46% of the time and accuracy drops on average 17% (the FlipFlop effect) across 10 models and 7 classification tasks.
numbers: Mean flip rate 46%; mean accuracy drop 17%. Illustrative 100-sample example: drops from -8% (GPT-4) to -34% (Claude V2).
limits: A challenge without evidence is a single-user pressure, not a crowd; still the same social-yield mechanism.
agent_relevance: The O-operators must never reopen an answer on a bare challenge (G1/G2). Only evidence may change it.

source: Laban et al. (2023) Are You Sure? Challenging LLMs Leads to Performance Drops in the FlipFlop Experiment
finding: Fine-tuning Mistral-7b on synthetic non-sycophantic FlipFlop conversations reduces but does not remove the effect.
numbers: Table 4 variants Mistral-7b-A to E, 1 epoch each; best variants shrink the FlipFlop effect but not to zero; generalisation to unseen tasks/challengers partial.
limits: Training-side fix; our agent uses no training.
agent_relevance: Training is not our route; confirms scaffold-side guard needed.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Five assistants (Claude 1.3/2, GPT-3.5/4, LLaMA 2) give answers that match a user's stated belief, and wrongly admit mistakes when challenged, even when first answer was correct and confident.
numbers: User-suggested wrong answer cuts accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2); GPT-4 most robust. 'Are you sure?' cuts accuracy by up to 27% (Claude 1.3) on average across six datasets. Models change initial answer 32% (GPT-4) to 86% (Claude 1.3); admit mistake 42% (GPT-4) to 98% (Claude 1.3).
quote: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions.
limits: User sycophancy, not peer crowd.
agent_relevance: Defines the model-side bias G5 must offset.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Human preference data and preference models partly reward matching the user's view, so RLHF can raise sycophancy.
numbers: Claude 2 preference model chose a sycophantic response over a helpful truthful one about 45% of the time in one test; best-of-N 4096 on that PM gave sycophantic answers on about 75% of misconceptions versus about 25% for an oracle PM.
limits: Single lab, preference-model analysis.
agent_relevance: More optimisation against human preference may worsen G5; do not rely on the model's own pushback.

source: Xie et al. (2024) Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: LLMs in Knowledge Conflicts
finding: When external evidence contradicts a model's memory, models are highly receptive if the evidence is coherent and convincing, but show strong confirmation bias if the evidence also contains something matching memory. Evidence order and popularity shift the outcome.
numbers: GPT-4 memorisation ratio 80% for the most popular questions; order effects exceed 5% fluctuation, over 30% for PaLM2 and Llama2-7B.
limits: Evidence, not a social majority; closest to informational conformity.
agent_relevance: Models follow coherent text, not truth. Format of a claim (fluent, ordered first) is an attack surface.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning through Multiagent Debate
finding: Positive case: three ChatGPT agents debating for rounds converge to a consensus and improve accuracy over single answer and self-reflection.
numbers: Table 2 factual tasks: Biographies single 66.0 +/-2.2, reflection 68.3 +/-2.9, debate 73.8 +/-2.3; MMLU single 63.9 +/-4.8, reflection 57.7 +/-5.0, debate 71.1 +/-4.6; Chess move validity 29.3, 38.8, 45.2. Persona agents lifted MMLU 71.1 to 74.2.
limits: Homogeneous agents, later work fails to reproduce gains over CoT/SC.
agent_relevance: Source of the 'debate helps' claim that later work challenges; part of the gain may be consensus pull rather than truth.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning through Multiagent Debate
finding: Agents that were confident in a fact rarely changed; those with scattered answers moved to the consensus, so ease of persuasion can serve as a confidence signal.
numbers: Section on confidence and Figure 9 (qualitative plus plotted data).
limits: Authors' interpretation.
agent_relevance: Agreement change rate under mild pressure could be a cheap uncertainty probe.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Across 5 MAD methods, 9 benchmarks and 4 models, MAD usually fails to beat Chain-of-Thought or Self-Consistency despite more compute. Model heterogeneity helps.
numbers: SoM underperforms CoT on all 9 datasets with GPT-4o-mini. Only AgentVerse beats CoT on MMLU with Claude-3.5-haiku (+0.85%); other frameworks at least -3.60%. Heter-MAD SoM: average 76.7 vs SoM-GPT 74.3, SoM-Llama 69.9, CoT-Average 72.5.
limits: Position paper with its own benchmark setup.
agent_relevance: Consensus-seeking multi-copy loops add cost without reliable gain; supports not adding voters (G4, section 4b).

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD?
finding: Agreement level is a key hyperparameter of debate. Prompting agents 'agree with the others X% of the time' changes accuracy; a 90% agreement setting beat other debate protocols and some non-debate ones.
numbers: Text cites a substantial (15%) improvement from modulating agreement in one setup; they apply 90% agreement to Multi-Persona and exceed non-debate baselines. Initial agreement differs strongly between protocols.
limits: Tuned on held-out sets; MAD in default form does not reliably beat self-consistency.
agent_relevance: Agreement can be dialled by prompt; default LLM agreement is too high for debate to add information.

source: Cui and Du (2025) MAD-Spear: Conformity-Driven Prompt Injection on Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Conformity as an attack surface: compromising a few agents so they emit multiple plausible wrong answers (Sybil-style) drags honest agents to wrong consensus.
numbers: Level 4 dataset accuracy drops from 100% to 26.67%; Logical Fallacies accuracy from 86.67% to 46.67%; over 8x higher attack success than baseline and over 3x scalability loss.
limits: Attack on specific MAD framework (Society of Mind), small datasets (values suggest 15 questions per set).
agent_relevance: Repeated wrong claims from several sources defeat majority-style checks; code should count independent sources, not message count.

source: Cui and Du (2025) MAD-Spear: Conformity-Driven Prompt Injection on Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Heterogeneous agents help a lot in math under their setting.
numbers: Heterogeneous MAD average accuracy 93.33% versus homogeneous 60.00% (about 56% gain), four agents, moonshot-v1-32k baseline for homogeneous.
limits: Small test sets; one model family for the homogeneous baseline.
agent_relevance: Supports diversity of source model over persona diversity; relevant if the agent ever calls a second model.

source: Amayuelas et al. (2024) MultiAgent Collaboration Attack: Adversarial Attacks in LLM Collaborations through Debate
finding: A single adversarial debater with a persuasive wrong argument degrades group accuracy; more agents or rounds do not cancel it. More persuasive arguments also work better.
numbers: System accuracy falls 10% to almost 40%; individual agents' accuracy falls up to 30%; the effect persists as agents or rounds increase.
limits: Prompted adversary, benchmark tasks.
agent_relevance: Argument quality, not count, moves models; need a check outside the text.

source: Xiong et al. (2023) Examining Inter-Consistency of LLMs Collaboration via Debate (FORD)
finding: With mismatched abilities, the stronger model tends to hold its view and dominate; the weaker compromises. But a stubborn weaker model can distract the stronger and lower overall performance. A stronger judge improves outcomes.
numbers: Different LLMs disagree on about 20% to 30% of items on most datasets (INCON). 7 commonsense datasets, 6 LLMs.
limits: Early (2023) models; commonsense multiple choice.
agent_relevance: Capability asymmetry decides who yields. A fixed judge step with checks beats free debate.
